problem: The transcription spells the Yankton speaker 'Pointed Bear', not Painted Bear (a different person, whose camp De Smet names). His words, as rendered, were that the Sioux did not understand the whites' manners or words, though they knew the proposals were meant for their good. The writer applied 'mere begging speeches' to 'several other Sioux' who spoke after these three, not to these three.

fix.digest: Mitchell asked for answers to his proposals and heard the Sioux first. A Brulé chief (rendered 'Terre Blue') said each band wanted its own chief and that his people were poor. Big Yankton said the travellers on the roads had destroyed the grass and timber and asked why the whites were not given grass of their own. Pointed Bear (so spelled), a Yankton, said they did not understand the whites' manners or words, though they knew the proposals were meant for their good. The writer dismissed several other Sioux speeches as 'mere begging speeches'.

problem: None of the fetched sources gives the date of the Senate vote. Kappler's note and the Forest Service's reference copy say only that the Senate ratified 'with an amendment changing the annuity in Article 7 from fifty to ten years, subject to acceptance by the tribes'. The amended article as printed allows continuation 'for a period not exceeding five years thereafter', so sources that give fifteen years are counting the discretionary extension. 24 May 1852 is plausible but was not seen in a fetched source. The statement that the next payment was held back until assent is not in Kappler.

fix.digest: Ratifying the treaty, the Senate amended Article 7 so that the $50,000 a year in goods would run for ten years instead of fifty, with the President free to continue it for up to five more (hence the 'fifteen years' in some accounts). The change was made subject to the nations' acceptance, and the task of getting it fell to the agents, Fitzpatrick for the Platte.

problem: Iti Fabvssa puts the reading of the revised treaty and the vote in LeFlore's district on the same day, the day after LeFlore's conditions (25 September). It gives no 26 September event. The day is inferred from 'the following day' and 'later that day'.

fix.digest: The revised treaty was read and translated to those still present, who talked loudly among themselves and showed no sign of signing. Later that day the commissioners put it to LeFlore's district alone. There too it failed, by about two to one, and those who voted against it went home thinking the business was finished. A newspaper correspondent heard that the vote in LeFlore's camp had been unanimous for holding on to the country.

problem: In the Duffy translation of the 25 December 1831 letter, the horses took fright and threw themselves into the river, and the dogs refused to board, howling, until their masters brought them aboard by force. The letter's comparison with the Spaniards concerns the belief that God had given the New World to the conquerors. The 'more humane and more destructive' judgement belongs to Democracy in America, not this letter. The excerpt does not name the boat or say where the letter was written.

fix.digest: Writing to his mother, Tocqueville described the boarding: horses that took fright and plunged into the river, dogs that howled and had to be carried aboard, a girl whose arm had been broken a week before, and a woman said to be 110 years old. He asked an English-speaking man why they were leaving and was told it was to be free. He likened the Americans' conviction that the New World was theirs by right to that of the Spanish conquerors.
